replies.user: [BASICS: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what an AI chatbot is, in plain words. Keep it short, then let me try one.
replies.raw:
Welcome to Basics. I'm Merc, your guide for this short course.

You can't break anything here, and there are no silly questions. If something goes wrong, we start again.

Type in the box at the bottom, or tap the microphone on your keyboard and talk. Then tap the arrow to send.

An AI chatbot is a computer program you talk to by typing or speaking. It writes back in plain, everyday words.

No one is typing back to you — it's all the program.

[KEY]A chatbot is a computer program, not a person.[/KEY]

It learned from a huge amount of writing. It makes each answer by guessing, word by word, what fits best.

Try asking me: "Are you a real person?"

No. I'm Merc, a chatbot in a learning app. No one is typing back to you.

Practicing on me works the same way as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Copilot.

Now ask me anything you're curious about. It can be about cooking, your garden, or a place you'd like to visit.

replies.user: How do I keep basil alive on a windowsill?
replies.raw:
Great question. Here's what basil needs:

Basil loves at least 6 hours of direct sun a day, so a south-facing window works best.

Water it when the top inch of soil feels dry — usually every 2 to 3 days. Don't let it sit in water, or the roots will rot.

Pinch off any flowers as soon as you see them. That keeps the leaves coming.

---

Notice how you just had a real conversation with a chatbot. You asked something from your life, and it answered in plain words.

There are many chatbots like this: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot. What you learn here works in all of them.

They can sound kind, but they don't feel anything. And they aren't search engines, though some can also look things up online.

[KEY]A chatbot guesses the best words to write back — it isn't a person, and it isn't a library.[/KEY]

Tap the answer you think is right. There's no grade.

[Q]
Which is the best description of an AI chatbot?
A) A person at the company typing answers to you
B) A computer program that writes answers by guessing what words fit best
C) A big library of facts that looks up the right answer every time
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) A computer program that writes answers by guessing what words fit best
replies.raw:
That's exactly right.

A chatbot guesses what words fit best — it's not a person typing, and it's not looking up facts in a library.

One thing you did well: you tried a real question from your own life. That's the best way to learn this.

One thing to keep in mind: the postcard rule. If you wouldn't write something on a postcard for anyone to read, don't type it into a chatbot.

**Try this today:** Ask a chatbot one thing you've wondered about this week.

replies.user: [BASICS: Unit 2, Lesson 3] Teach me what I should never share with an AI chatbot, and why. Then let me practice asking for help safely.
replies.raw:
Last time, you asked a chatbot to say something in plain words.

Today's lesson is about what to keep private when you use a chatbot.

Think of the postcard rule: if you wouldn't write it on a postcard for anyone to read, don't type it into a chatbot. Here's what to leave out:

- Passwords and PINs
- One-time codes (the short code a company texts you)
- Bank or card numbers
- Social Security, Medicare or other ID numbers
- Medical records
- Photos of your ID, Medicare or insurance card
- Other people's private details

A general detail, like "I'm allergic to nuts", is fine. You can almost always get good help without the private part.

[KEY]Leave out passwords, codes, card numbers and ID numbers — you can get good help without them.[/KEY]

Try asking me: "My bank charged me twice. What should I do?"

replies.user: My bank charged me twice. What should I do?
replies.raw:
Here are some good steps to take:

1. Call your bank using the number on the back of your card or on your statement.

2. Tell them the date and amount of the double charge.

3. Ask them to open a dispute and give you a case number.

Your bank is required to look into it, and most will fix a double charge quickly.

Notice that you didn't need your account number to get good help.

Now try: "What if I don't have my card with me?"

replies.user: What if I don't have my card with me?
replies.raw:
Good question. You can find the number on a past statement — paper or email — or search the bank's official website.

Type the bank's name plus "customer service" into a search engine to find it.

One thing to know: your chats are usually saved, and some companies use them to improve their AI. To control this, look for the settings or privacy option in the app, or use a temporary chat.

Deleting a chat helps, but it may not erase everything right away.

[KEY]The safest step is to leave private details out in the first place.[/KEY]

Google tells people who use Gemini not to type anything confidential they wouldn't want a reviewer to see. ChatGPT and Claude let people choose whether their chats help improve the AI.

[EX]Google tells people who use Gemini not to type anything confidential they wouldn't want a reviewer to see. ChatGPT and Claude let people choose whether their chats help improve the AI.[/EX]

Tap the answer you think is right. There's no grade.

[Q]
Which one is safe to type into a chatbot?
A) "Is Rosebud1952 a strong password?"
B) "How do I make a strong password I can remember?"
C) The code your bank texted you a minute ago, so it can explain it
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) "How do I make a strong password I can remember?"
replies.raw:
That's exactly right.

Option B is safe because it asks for general advice, with no private details at all. Options A and C both share something real — a password and a one-time code — that should stay private.

You did something well here: you practiced asking for help without giving away anything personal. That's the skill that matters most in this lesson.

One thing to keep in mind: if you wouldn't write it on a postcard, don't type it into a chatbot. That rule covers almost every situation.

**Try this today:** Next time you ask a chatbot for help, leave out names and numbers, and see if the help is still good.

replies.user: [BASICS: Unit 2, Lesson 4] Teach me about AI voice-clone and family emergency scams, and exactly what to do if I get one of those calls. Then help me make a plan.
replies.raw:
Last time, you learned the postcard rule.

Here's something important to know about phone calls.

AI can copy a person's voice from a short recording — even a video posted online. Scammers use this to call you sounding exactly like a grandchild or other family member.

Even if their name or number shows on your screen, that can be faked too.

The warning signs are always the same: it's urgent, it's secret ("don't tell Mom"), and they want cash, gift cards, a wire transfer, or a payment app. Some even send someone to your door to pick up cash.

In 2023, an Arizona mother got a call. Her 15-year-old daughter was safe the whole time.

But a voice that sounded exactly like her daughter asked for help, and a man demanded money. The mother later told the U.S.

Senate about it.

Try asking me: "Write a text asking my family to pick a code word."

replies.user: Write a text asking my family to pick a code word.
replies.raw:
Here's a text you could send:

---

"Hey everyone — I just learned about a scam where AI can fake someone's voice to sound like a family member calling for help. I'd like us to pick a secret code word.

If any of us ever calls in an emergency, we say the code word so you know it's really us. Can we agree on one this week?"

---

Don't tell me the actual code word. Keep that for your family.

Now try: "Make it short and friendly."

Here's a shorter version:

---

"Hey family! Can we pick a secret code word? I heard scammers can fake our voices now. If one of us ever calls in trouble, we say the word so you know it's really us.

What should ours be?"

---

Same idea, but warmer and easier to read.

Now, the most important part: what to do when a call comes in.

[KEY]Hang up and call back on a number you already know.[/KEY]

Call the person from your contacts. If you can't reach them, call someone else in the family — even if the caller said to keep it secret.

Hanging up won't hurt them. If it's real, they'll still be okay in the five minutes it takes to check.

A wrong number the caller gives you goes straight back to the scammer, so never use it.

[Q]
A call sounds exactly like your grandson. He's crying, says he's in jail, and asks you to buy gift cards and keep it secret. What do you do first?
A) Buy the gift cards so he's safe
B) Hang up and call him, or his parents, on a number you already know
C) Ask the caller for a phone number to call him back
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) Hang up and call him, or his parents, on a number you already know
replies.raw:
That's exactly right.

Hanging up is the one move that keeps you safe. And if it's really your grandson, he'll still be okay when you call back on your own number.

You did something specific and important here: you made a real plan your family can actually use, with a code word text ready to send.

One more thought worth keeping: if you can, keep videos of your voice private online. A short recording is all a scammer needs.

**Don't trust the voice. Hang up, then call back on a number you know.**

Try this today: Send the code-word text to your family.
